verses.text: And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ.
I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able.
For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?
For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?
Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.
Now he that planteth and he that watereth are one: and every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour.
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building.
According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble;
Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is.
If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward.
If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.
Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?
If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.
Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.
Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours;
Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours;
And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s.

summary: Paul has already named the Corinthian factions; here he diagnoses them. He tells them he "could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ," having fed them "with milk, and not with meat" because they were not able to bear it — "neither yet now are ye able." The proof of their infancy is not ignorance of doctrine but the temper of their common life: "whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?" Party slogans are the symptom, and Paul takes the first of them as his own indictment: "while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?" His answer deflates both names at once — "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?" — and then supplies the image that governs the rest of the chapter: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." Because growth belongs to God, "neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth," yet the workers are not thereby erased; they "are one," and "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour." The field turns into a construction site: "ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building." Paul describes himself as "a wise masterbuilder" who has "laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon," with a warning attached — "let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon" — since "other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." What is built on that foundation will be sorted by fire: some raise "gold, silver, precious stones," others "wood, hay, stubble," and "the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is." Work that abides earns "a reward"; work that burns means real loss, "but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." The building then proves to be a sanctuary: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" — and the party spirit tearing at that community is no small matter, for "if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are." Paul closes by inverting the very thing the factions were competing over. "Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise," because "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God," as the scriptures testify: "He taketh the wise in their own craftiness," and "The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." The conclusion turns their arithmetic inside out — they had been dividing themselves up among teachers, when in fact "all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s."
takeaways: Spiritual maturity is measured here by how a community behaves, not by how much it knows. Paul calls the Corinthians "carnal" and "babes in Christ" and names the evidence plainly: "envying, and strife, and divisions." They are not accused of heresy or immorality at this point, only of factionalism — which turns out to be enough. To "walk as men" is to run a church by the ordinary logic of rival loyalties and personalities, and Paul treats that as a diet problem: people still on "milk, and not with meat" cannot digest the deeper teaching, and the reason is moral rather than intellectual.

The chapter dismantles celebrity ministry without dismissing ministers. "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed" strips the names of any claim to be sources; "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" locates all fruitfulness in God alone. Yet the same passage refuses to make the workers irrelevant: they "are one," not competitors, they are "labourers together with God," and "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour." Genuine human effort is real and will be genuinely rewarded, precisely because it is not the cause of the growth and therefore has nothing to protect.

There is exactly one foundation and unlimited responsibility for what is raised on it. "Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ" closes the question of the church’s basis permanently, but that settled foundation makes the next sentence more urgent rather than less: "let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon." The contrast between "gold, silver, precious stones" and "wood, hay, stubble" is not a contrast between true and false religion — all of it is built on Christ — but between work that survives testing and work that does not. Being on the right foundation is no guarantee of building well.

Judgment is described as revelation before it is described as punishment. "Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is." The fire is an assayer, not primarily an executioner; its function is to show "of what sort" the work is. And the outcome for the builder whose work fails is stated with striking restraint — "he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." Real loss and real salvation are held together in a single verse, which is why this text has carried so much weight in later argument about what happens to a saved person’s unworthy work.

The community itself is the sanctuary, and damaging it is sacrilege. "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" is addressed to a whole congregation in the plural, so the temple in view is the assembled church before it is the individual believer. That is what raises the stakes of mere partisanship to "If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy." Faction-building is not a matter of poor manners in a voluntary society; it is defacing a holy place, and the reason given is simply what the place is: "the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are."

The remedy for competitive wisdom is a deliberate self-emptying. "If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise" asks for a real surrender of standing, not a rhetorical pose, and it is grounded in a verdict already rendered: "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." The chapter’s final turn then exposes how small the factions had made themselves. In claiming a teacher they had been dividing an inheritance that was already entirely theirs — "all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come" — and the whole chain is anchored where boasting cannot reach: "ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 1:10-31 — every one of you saith, I am of Paul... but God hath chosen the foolish things of the world
crossRefs.why: The opening chapter states the problem this one diagnoses: the same slogans, the same names, and the same collision between "the wisdom of this world" and the preaching of a crucified Christ. Read together, the two chapters show that Paul treats Corinthian factionalism and Corinthian admiration for clever speech as a single disorder, which is why he answers party spirit with a doctrine of God-given increase rather than with a compromise between the parties.

crossRefs.label: Acts 18 — Paul... continued there a year and six months... and Apollos... mightily convinced the Jews
crossRefs.why: Luke supplies the history behind "I have planted, Apollos watered." Paul founded the Corinthian congregation over eighteen months, and the eloquent Alexandrian arrived afterward and helped the believers greatly. Knowing that both men actually worked in sequence rather than in rivalry sharpens Paul’s point that the factions had invented a competition their supposed champions never had.

crossRefs.label: Job 5:13 — He taketh the wise in their own craftiness
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this line directly as scriptural proof that "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." The original setting is a speech about God overturning the schemes of the crafty and lifting the lowly, which is the same reversal Paul is applying to Corinthian factions built on admiration for skilled speakers.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 2:19-22 — built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone... an holy temple in the Lord
crossRefs.why: The same two images — foundation and temple — are joined there as here, with the building described as growing into "an habitation of God through the Spirit." The parallel confirms that Paul’s "ye are God’s building" and "ye are the temple of God" describe one corporate structure made of people, and it clarifies how the apostolic foundation-laying of this chapter relates to Christ as the foundation itself.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 5:10 — we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body
crossRefs.why: Paul later states as bare doctrine what he here dramatizes with fire and building materials: believers are assessed for what they have done. Set beside "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour" and "the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is," it establishes that a judgment of works applies to the saved and not only to the lost.

crossRefs.label: Malachi 3:2-3 — for he is like a refiner’s fire... and he shall purify the sons of Levi
crossRefs.why: The prophet describes the Lord’s coming to his temple as a refining that purges rather than destroys, so that offerings may be made "in righteousness." Catholic reading hears that refining note in "the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire" and especially in "he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire," where the person passes through the fire and comes out purified rather than condemned.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in "If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire" one of the clearest scriptural pointers toward a purification after death. The person in view is neither condemned nor waved through: he is saved, yet he genuinely suffers loss, and he passes through fire to arrive there. Since the fire is said to "try every man’s work of what sort it is" and the deficient work is destroyed while the builder survives, the tradition reads the passage as describing a real purgative experience for those who die in grace but with attachments and unworthy work still clinging to them. Set alongside the chapter’s temple language — "the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are" — the argument is that holiness is not merely imputed at the threshold but actually completed, and that this passage shows the completing as costly.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the fire here as the eschatological judgment of Christ’s appearing rather than an intermediate state. The stated subject of the testing is the work, not the worker — "the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is" — and "the day shall declare it" points to a single public day of assessment, so the loss described is the loss of reward for ministry poorly built, not a period of personal expiation. The phrase "yet so as by fire" is taken as an image of narrow escape, like a man running out of a burning house with nothing but his life, which underlines that his salvation rests wholly on the one foundation already laid and not on the quality of what he built. Both traditions agree that the believer is truly saved, that the loss is real, and that the entire scene presupposes salvation grounded in Christ rather than in the surviving work.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "For we are labourers together with God" states a genuine cooperation between divine grace and human action, and the chapter holds that cooperation in balance rather than resolving it in one direction. God alone "gave the increase," so no minister is a source of anything; and yet "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour," which presupposes that the labour is truly the man’s own and truly counts. Catholic tradition takes this as the shape of merit: what is rewarded is God’s grace at work in a free human agent, so that crediting the reward to the labourer and crediting the growth to God are not competing claims. The ministers are read as real instrumental causes — "ministers by whom ye believed" — through whom God ordinarily gives what only he can give.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters emphasize the negative half of the same argument, where Paul says that "neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase." On this reading the point of the planting-and-watering image is to reduce the workers to nothing precisely so that boasting in men becomes impossible — "therefore let no man glory in men" — and the rewards that follow are understood as God graciously crowning his own gifts rather than as wages the labourer has earned. The distinction usually drawn is between reward, which this chapter clearly promises to believers, and merit understood as a claim on God, which Protestants deny while affirming that works done in faith are truly assessed and truly rewarded. Both traditions affirm that God alone gives growth, that ministers are instruments rather than sources, and that faithful labour is not wasted.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
